paragraph: Section 110 (24 August, pp. 443–445) reopens schematization through the functor $W(M)(k)=M\otimes_{\underline{Z}}k$, vector bundles, semisimplicial abelian groups, and Postnikov fibrations. The page explicitly returns to the ground-ring discussion at the end of section 94 (p. 444). Grothendieck first investigates constructing a schematic homotopy type from its successive homotopy groups, then on p. 444 invokes the universal-coefficient difficulty caused by homology torsion and withdraws confidence in that construction. The handwritten replacement of the displayed identification of homology with homotopy by ``or rather is consequential here: the arXiv witness retains the equality wording (concordance D09258). The same page turns toward abelianization or linearization with extra multiplicative structure; section 111 begins a new approach through unipotent bundles (p. 446). Page 445 reflects on the preceding hundred pages of abelianization and on his decision not to complete a perfectly symmetric notation for all Hom and tensor operations. This records the status of the investigation and the reason for the next construction; the proposed schematization has not been established in this section.

Section 111 (25 August, pp. 446–459) proposes categories of schematic homotopy types through semisimplicial unipotent bundles. The objects are first approached as iterated torsors under the functors $W(M)$, with a choice between retaining a filtration and taking a coarser category $U(k)$ (pp. 446–448). The proposed models impose conditions on low degrees, and the initial weak equivalences are tested on the semisimplicial sets of $k$-valued points (p. 449). A proposed comparison with the derived category leads to a linearization constructed from divided-power algebras, first completed and then in a pointed version $L_{pt}$ (pp. 450–454). Question 1 compares this construction with ordinary abelianization; the margin of p. 452 explicitly adds $k=\underline{Z}$ and projective components. The following pages explain these revisions. The discussion of chain complexes and Kan--Dold--Puppe on pp. 455–456 corrects the earlier calculation of the derived divided-power functor by requiring a projective resolution, and turns from literal Postnikov layers to models built from projective, or possibly flat, modules. The second afterthought on pp. 457–458 reexamines the ground ring: the example $k=\underline{Z}[T]/(T^2+1)$ is used to challenge the earlier proposed $k$-module structure on ordinary integral homology. Page 458 then considers defining weak equivalences through the linearization and its homology invariants. Its handwritten phrase “becoming dubious” is consequential: the witness has “becoming obvious” (D09510). Question 2 on p. 459 asks about comparison with the earlier definition and emphasizes the conditions $X_0=X_1=e$. These remain questions in the text. Section 112 resumes them from the Eilenberg--MacLane case and the proposed Kan--Postnikov models (p. 460). Smaller formula variants requiring care are the two-prime chain-complex reference on p. 455 (D09441), the plain printed $I_k$ on p. 456 where the witness has $L_k$ (D09456), and the $m$ subscript of the model category on p. 448 followed by $n$ on p. 449; the edition preserves these page readings.
